prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which established the basis for incretin-based therapies of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part on B028 for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The first-round exchange did not move the scientific case, which rests on a complete arc from proglucagon processing and the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, through glucose-dependent insulin secretion and the effects on appetite and gastric emptying, to drugs with benefit confirmed in large independent outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease. The mechanism is stable and the clinical effect is still growing, so timing is not a concern. What the exchange did sharpen is the framing. The chair's first question is the real one: the citation should honour the physiology and the identification of the active peptide, and say so in words, so that the absence of the drug-design step reads as a principled choice and not as an oversight. Holst (human GLP-1 physiology), Drucker (GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology and the gut-hormone axis) and Mojsov (the active peptide) are the discovery-side names, and that trio fills the three seats without needing a second part. Five of six members now converge on it, but I hold it for the discovery chain and not for the count.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point and the exchange did not remove it. Habener is not among the credited names, and every member has flagged him; whichever trio we choose is open to the charge that it settles a disputed priority by omission. Mojsov's claim to the active peptide is contested, and the supplied text cannot decide it, so my support for her rests partly on recollection that I have not verified. The alternative reading, which Linnarsson makes well, is that converting a peptide with a half-life of minutes into a once-weekly drug needed new insight, so a physiology-only citation may be seen as honouring the preliminaries and passing over the step that reached patients. Lastly, the commercial scale of this drug class, and open questions about durability after discontinuation and long-term safety, mean the citation should stay anchored in discovery, not in market success.

responses.point: Linnarsson holds Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, arguing that turning native GLP-1 into a once-weekly agent through albumin binding and DPP-4 resistance was an inventive step and not routine engineering, while accepting that the physiology-only trio is the main competing configuration.
responses.response: Your point about albumin binding and DPP-4 resistance moves me on one thing: I no longer describe Knudsen's work as engineering on a settled target, and I accept that it was inventive. It does not move me on the seat. The question I am answering is which contribution the prize should name, and the discovery that made the drug class possible is the identification of the active peptide and its physiology. Your own position that Knudsen over Mojsov is not a point of principle suggests the gap between us is small. Where I would not follow you is on resolving Mojsov's contested priority by removing her; that would swap one attribution problem for a different one and would drop the only credited person tied to the active peptide. I would reopen the third seat only if a clear majority wants a therapy-framed citation, and then the names and the citation would need to change together, not just one seat.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, moved from Drucker, Holst and Knudsen to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, reasoning that the citation can then reward discovery of the hormone's physiology and active form and not a company's drug design.
responses.response: I welcome the move and I think the reasoning is sound, but I want to hold you to its implication, which I raised in round 1: if Knudsen is left out, the citation must state that the award is for physiology and the active form. I have worded my citation that way. On your second-round question about Habener, I do not think his absence from the credited names alters which trio is defensible, but it should shape how we write the rationale, since the committee will be judged on how it treats the proglucagon and early GLP-1 work. I would not weaken Mojsov's place because of it. On a second part, I agree with your view that B020 needs a narrow citation around IRE1, HAC1 and XBP1 if it is ever taken up, and for the same reason I would not stretch B028 to carry a fourth name.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius holds that Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is documented well enough to justify credit, and that excluding her would risk an attribution mistake the field would remember; she would accept Knudsen if a majority wanted a therapy-oriented citation.
responses.response: I agree with you on Mojsov and with your preference that the allocation be discussed openly and not treated as settled. I am less convinced by your worry that B045 sits on cleaner ground than B028. A June and Sadelain pair is cleaner on the page, but Eshhar's omission is a real gap in the record and the committee would still be fixing names before agreeing what the achievement is. B045 is a stronger case than B020 on clinical maturity, as you argue, and it is my first alternative. But I do not think its cleaner pairing outweighs the completeness of the incretin chain, and I would not move a second part into this year's prize, because B028 already uses the full three-name limit. If the committee does reach a two-part prize in some other form, I would want it to be June and Sadelain only.

responses.point: El Manira argues that a prize rewarding a drug class with a very large commercial footprint risks being read as rewarding commercial success, that long-term safety and durability after discontinuation remain open, and that Walter and Mori for the unfolded protein response is the cleanest basic-science pair.
responses.response: You are right that the commercial footprint is a risk, and it is one reason I want the citation framed around physiology and the active peptide, not around the products. I share your view that safety and durability are still being defined, but I do not think that is disqualifying: the discovery and the mechanism are settled, and the open questions concern the use of the drugs, not the biology. On B020, we agree that it is the most conceptually original alternative and has the cleanest attribution. What separates us is maturity. For it to move ahead of B045 I would want a clearer disease link, which I do not yet see, so B020 stays my second alternative. It would be my choice if the committee decides that conceptual clarity of credit counts more than therapeutic reach, and I would word it narrowly around the IRE1-HAC1-XBP1 mechanism, as Svenningsson says.

responses.point: Perlmann would change his view only if the committee decides the citation should be about the therapy, in which case Holst, Drucker and Knudsen is defensible, and he still wants Habener's role dealt with; he also rates B037 below B045 and B014 for a first prize.
responses.response: I agree with the conditional you set out, and I would apply it to myself in the same way: the trio and the citation are one decision. On Habener we agree that it cannot be resolved from the supplied text, and I would add that neither of us can resolve it from memory, so the committee should avoid asserting a priority ruling and should word the citation to describe what the credited three did without claiming that nobody else contributed. On B037 I accept your point that its credited names omit earlier SMN2 oligonucleotide work, and that it drew little support in the other openings; I drop it as a named alternative and keep B045 and B020 as my two, because both drew clear support from several members. I also agree that B014 cannot be cut to three names honestly this year.

uncertainties: Whether the supplied record supports Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide well enough to hold the third seat; my account is from recollection and has not been checked against primary sources.
How the committee should treat Habener's absence from the credited names, and whether the citation wording alone can avoid implying a priority ruling.

Whether a majority will prefer a therapy-oriented citation, which would move the third seat to Knudsen. I would reopen the allocation in that case, but I would insist that the citation and the names change together.
Whether the long-term safety and durability questions, and the commercial scale of the drug class, will affect how the prize is read by outside observers, even if they do not affect the science.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. No shortlisted candidate has a documented connection to me. I have co-authored work with committee colleagues Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisén and share Karolinska Institutet with other members, but none of this involves a credited name on any shortlisted ballot, and I do not infer a personal tie from shared affiliation or topic. I report no recusal issue.
